subject: Economics
topic: GDP, GVA and national accounting — mixed tiers
description: GDP at market price vs factor cost, GVA, real vs nominal, deflator, current rank

questions.stem: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) measures the value of all final goods and services produced:

options.option_text: By Indian residents anywhere in the world
Within a country's geographic boundaries during a given period
Only by Indian citizens abroad
By the government only

questions.explanation: GDP — based on geography (where produced). GNP (Gross National Product) — based on nationality of producer (Indian residents anywhere in world). GNP = GDP + NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad). NFIA can be positive (Saudi Arabia, US — get income from abroad) or negative (India — net outflow as we have more foreign investment than Indians earning abroad). Most countries report GDP as the primary aggregate.

questions.stem: The relation between 'GDP at Market Price' (GDPmp) and 'GDP at Factor Cost' (GDPfc) is:

options.option_text: GDPmp = GDPfc + Indirect taxes − Subsidies
GDPmp = GDPfc + Subsidies − Indirect taxes
GDPmp = GDPfc − Profits
GDPmp = GDPfc + Depreciation

questions.explanation: Net Indirect Taxes (NIT) = Indirect taxes − Subsidies. GDPmp = GDPfc + NIT. The 'wedge' between the two reflects taxes (which add to market price) and subsidies (which lower it). GDPfc is sometimes called 'income approach' GDP (sum of factor incomes — wages, rent, interest, profit). Net vs Gross — subtract depreciation to get NDP / NNP from GDP / GNP.

questions.stem: Since 2015, India's primary headline national-income measure as published by MoSPI is:

options.option_text: GDP at factor cost (old base)
GDP at constant market prices + GVA at basic prices (2011-12 base)
GNP only
Per-capita income

questions.explanation: MoSPI revised the base year to 2011-12 (from 2004-05) in January 2015. Headline became GDP at MARKET PRICES (constant) for international comparability. Sectoral analysis switched to GVA at BASIC PRICES — 'basic price' = factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies (excludes net product taxes). Relationship: GVA basic prices + Net product taxes = GDP market prices. Quarterly + advance estimates released regularly. Latest 2024-25 GDP growth ~7.6% (real).

questions.stem: The 'GDP deflator' is best described as:

options.option_text: Same as CPI
Ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP — broadest measure of economy-wide inflation
Always equals 100
Inflation in foreign-trade goods only

questions.explanation: GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. It captures price changes across ALL goods/services in the economy (not just consumer basket like CPI). Nominal GDP at current prices → reflects both volume + price changes. Real GDP at base-year prices → reflects only volume change. Wider than CPI (consumer-only) and WPI (wholesale only). Implicit measure — derived rather than directly polled. Useful for cross-country comparisons of long-term inflation trends.

questions.stem: By nominal GDP rank in 2025-26 (per IMF / Economic Survey), India is the:

options.option_text: 5th largest economy
4th largest economy (overtook Japan in FY 2024-25)
3rd largest economy
10th largest economy

questions.explanation: India overtook Japan to become the 4th largest economy by nominal GDP in FY 2024-25 (~USD 4 trillion). The order: USA (~28T) > China (~18T) > Germany (~4.5T) > India (~4T) > Japan (~4T very close). On PPP basis India is already 3rd (after US, China). Aim — 3rd largest by 2027-28 when India would overtake Germany (~$5 T projected). Per-capita GDP however is much lower — India ~$2,800 vs Germany $54,000 (2024).

questions.stem: Three approaches to compute GDP — Production / Income / Expenditure — should all give:

options.option_text: Different numbers
The same total (income earned = output produced = expenditure on output)
Average of two methods
Maximum of the three

questions.explanation: Three sides of the same coin (Circular Flow of Income): (1) Production / Output / Value-Added = sum of GVA across all industries. (2) Income = sum of factor payments — wages + rent + interest + profit + mixed income. (3) Expenditure = C (consumption) + I (investment) + G (government) + X − M (net exports). All three measure the same economy → same total. In practice, statistical discrepancy arises but is reconciled. India officially uses Output approach for GDP and Expenditure-side for double-checking.

questions.stem: Net National Product at factor cost (NNPfc) — popularly called 'National Income' — is calculated as:

options.option_text: GNPmp − Depreciation − Indirect taxes + Subsidies
GDP at market price + Indirect taxes
GDP at factor cost − Subsidies
Per-capita income × population

questions.explanation: Hierarchy from GDP to National Income: GDP at market price → +NFIA → GNP at market price → −Depreciation → NNP at market price → −Indirect taxes + Subsidies → NNP at factor cost (= National Income). Per-capita income = NNPfc / population. India's per-capita NNI (2024-25) ≈ ₹2.0 lakh at current prices.

questions.stem: Which formula correctly links Gross Value Added (GVA) at basic prices to GDP at market prices?

options.option_text: GDP (MP) = GVA + Subsidies − Product taxes
GDP (MP) = GVA + Product taxes − Subsidies
GDP (MP) = GVA − Product taxes + Subsidies
GDP (MP) = GVA + Net Factor Income from Abroad

questions.explanation: GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + Taxes on products − Subsidies on products (i.e., + Net taxes on products). Option A reverses the sign, incorrectly netting subsidies above taxes. Option D confuses the GVA→GDP step with the GDP→GNP step; adding NFIA converts GDP to GNP, not GVA to GDP.

questions.stem: Net Domestic Product (NDP) at market prices is obtained from GDP at market prices by?

options.option_text: Adding net indirect taxes levied on domestic output
Subtracting depreciation (capital consumption allowance)
Adding net factor income earned from abroad by residents
Subtracting net exports from the total expenditure side

questions.explanation: NDP = GDP − Depreciation (Capital Consumption Allowance), which accounts for wear and tear of fixed capital used in production. Option C describes how GDP converts to GNP via the NFIA adjustment — a common confusion. Net indirect taxes are already embedded in GDP at MP, so adding them again (Option A) would double-count.

questions.stem: Output of a Japanese-owned factory operating inside Indian territory will be counted in which national accounts?

options.option_text: Counted in both India's GDP and India's GNP
Counted in India's GDP and also in Japan's GNP
Counted in India's GNP and also in Japan's GDP
Counted in both Japan's GDP and Japan's GNP

questions.explanation: GDP covers production within a country's geographic boundary; GNP covers production by a country's nationals wherever located. The factory is on Indian soil → India's GDP. It is owned by Japanese nationals → Japan's GNP. It is excluded from India's GNP (non-Indian ownership) and from Japan's GDP (not on Japanese territory). Option A is the most common wrong answer — students forget that GNP strips out foreign-owned production.

questions.stem: Transfer payments such as old-age pensions and unemployment allowances are excluded from GDP primarily because?

options.option_text: They are paid out of government budgets and not by private firms
They do not correspond to any current production of goods or services
They are already captured under the household consumption component
They represent capital expenditure rather than revenue expenditure

questions.explanation: GDP measures the value of current economic production. Transfer payments are one-sided flows — the recipient provides no good or service in return — so including them would inflate income without any matching output. Option C is wrong: it is the household's subsequent spending of that transferred income that enters consumption — the transfer itself is not a transaction for production.

questions.stem: The base year adopted by MoSPI for India's current National Accounts Statistics series (launched in January 2015) is?

options.option_text: 2004-05, which was the base year of the previous CSO series
2011-12, adopted under the revised National Accounts series
2014-15, aligned with the Rangarajan Committee revision year
2017-18, updated to reflect the post-GST economic structure

questions.explanation: In January 2015, CSO (now MoSPI) shifted India's National Accounts base year from 2004-05 to 2011-12. The same revision replaced GDP at factor cost with GVA at basic prices as the headline measure. Option A is the old (superseded) base year — the most tempting distractor for candidates who studied from pre-2015 material.

questions.stem: Gross National Disposable Income (GNDI) exceeds Gross National Product (GNP) when a country receives positive net?

options.option_text: Net indirect taxes collected by the central government
Net current transfers received from the rest of the world
Net fixed capital formation over the depreciation provision
Net factor income earned abroad by resident nationals

questions.explanation: GNDI = GNP + Net Current Transfers from Abroad (e.g., remittances, foreign grants). These transfers raise disposable income without representing factor payments for production. Option D is the critical distractor: NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad) is what converts GDP into GNP — so it is already embedded in GNP and cannot be the further step that gives GNDI. For India, massive inward remittances consistently make GNDI > GNP.

questions.stem: India's GDP measured at Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) is substantially larger than at current market exchange rates mainly because?

options.option_text: PPP also captures informal sector output omitted from official GDP data
Non-traded goods and services are relatively cheaper in India than in the US
The rupee is systematically overvalued against the dollar in forex markets
PPP calculations incorporate projected real growth of emerging economies

questions.explanation: PPP equalises price levels using a common basket of goods. In India, non-tradables (local food, housing, personal services) cost far less in rupee terms than their dollar equivalents in the US — the Balassa-Samuelson effect. PPP conversion captures this higher real purchasing power, raising India's PPP-GDP relative to market-rate GDP. Option C is wrong: the rupee is typically undervalued on forex markets (which would actually raise market-rate GDP), and PPP addresses price-level differences, not currency misalignment. Option A conflates PPP methodology with informal-sector measurement.
